title: POC scoping — load signature, QPS & concurrency modeling (Sentinel Analytics)
summary: Discovery and POC scoping focused on defining a workload signature and traffic model for a 6-week proof-of-concept. Key success criteria: tail latency < 300ms p50 for small prompts, p95 < 1s for typical inference; cost target within 30% of current hosted spend; KV/prefix cache reduces tokens by >15% on average. Agreed next steps include sample dataset drop, benchmark plan, and a 48-hour perf run on Redwood Dedicated with 2 replica pools.
next_steps: Redwood to share benchmark plan and runner script by 2025-08-21
Customer to upload 2k representative prompts + tokenized stats to shared S3 by 2025-08-22
Follow-up sync to review results on 2025-08-29
action_items: Samir Patel: Send cost modeling spreadsheet and example workload template by 2025-08-21
Elena Rodriguez: Prepare benchmark runner and Docker image, include client-side QPS generator by 2025-08-21
Priya Shah: Drop 2,000 representative prompts and a small token histogram CSV into shared S3 by 2025-08-22
Mark Turner: Provide network egress limits and VPC peering info for Dedicated trial by 2025-08-22
Luis Gomez: Confirm firewall rules and IP allowlist window for 48-hour run by 2025-08-24
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-19
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Elena (Redwood SE), Jordan (Redwood SA), Priya (Sentinel Head of ML), Mark (Platform), Luis (SRE), Alex (PM), Anika (Data Privacy)

[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for taking time today. Quick roll call?
[00:12] Priya: Hi, Priya here. Sorry ran a bit behind, thanks for accommodating.
[00:15] Mark: Mark Turner, Platform.
[00:18] Luis: Luis, SRE.
[00:20] Alex: Alex, product.
[00:21] Anika: Anika, privacy.
[00:23] Samir: Great, from Redwood, Elena and Jordan are with me. Elena will lead the technical baseline and Jordan will cover the Dedicated footprint options.
[00:42] Elena: Thanks. High level agenda for folks: we want to capture a workload signature — QPS, concurrency, input vs output token histogram, latencies you care about — and then map that to a short POC plan so you can validate cost and tail behavior. Does that align?
[01:10] Priya: Yes, that's the goal. We're shipping a summarization and extraction endpoint for the platform — it's used by our analytics customers to get entity extraction and short summarization. Expected pattern is a mix: about 70% short prompts (~50-120 input tokens) with relatively small outputs (20-60 tokens), and 30% longer prompts (300-800 input tokens) with larger outputs (100-400). But that's roughly, we need better numbers.
[01:42] Samir: Perfect. Can you give us current QPS and traffic shape? Spiky? Steady?
[01:55] Priya: At the moment, in staging we see baseline of 12-18 rps, spikes to 160 rps for 3-7 minutes for peak jobs — batch ingestion combined with interactive queries. Production on-peak might be higher but we haven't simulated spikes fully.
[02:15] Elena: Ok, so for the POC we should model both steady-state and spike windows. Two parts: 1) a 48-hour steady run at your 99th percentile expected daily QPS, and 2) synthetic spike windows that simulate the 3-7 minute bursts to observe queueing and tail latency.
[02:35] Mark: What's your recommended concurrency for the Dedicated nodes for that workload?
[02:45] Jordan: It depends on model choice and GPU. But practical starting point is 4–8 concurrent inflight requests per GPU for longer-context models; for short prompts you can push higher with batching. We'll propose a profile and we can tune.
[03:05] Alex: Quick question on caching: Priya mentioned prefix caching earlier — how much improvement is realistic?
[03:15] Elena: In our experience, KV/prefix caching can reduce per-request tokens by ~10–30% depending on prompt repetitiveness. For templated prompts like your extraction calls, we often see >15% token savings. But need sample prompts to estimate more accurately.
[03:35] Priya: We'll share a sample set. We can also export a tokenized histogram from our tokenizer.
[03:42] Samir: Great, that helps the cost model. Our success criteria—what should we lock in? We typically see customers want latency SLOs and cost windows. What are yours?
[03:57] Priya: For this POC, acceptance would be: p50 < 200–300ms for short prompts, p95 < 1s for typical interactive load, and no more than 5% requests with errors/timeouts during spike windows. Cost target is to be within 30% of our current hosted spend using a similar quality model. Also need to validate that tokenized cost and billing breakdown maps to our accounting.
[04:25] Elena: Sounds reasonable. We'll include a billing trace for the runs and a token-level breakdown. We'll also include a tail-latency histogram so you can compare p50/p95/p99.
[04:40] Anika: On privacy and security, we need to understand data residency/retention for logs, and where request payloads land during the Dedicated trial. We prefer VPC peering for the Dedicated run.
[04:55] Jordan: Dedicated supports VPC peering and private deployment options; for the 48-hour run we can do a temporary peered environment. We'll need your IP ranges and a maintenance window to open firewall rules.
[05:12] Luis: We'll need a list of outbound IPs to allow. Also confirm if logs will be delivered to our S3 or retained by Redwood console.
[05:25] Elena: We can stream request-level logs to your S3 bucket for the trial; we can also keep an operational copy in the console for 7 days. We'll capture only non-sensitive metadata by default unless you instruct us otherwise.
[05:42] Priya: Good. For the bench we're fine sending anonymized prompts, but some prompts are PII-heavy. We'll do tokenized/stubbed variants for those.
[05:55] Samir: That's reasonable. Let's move to the benchmark methodology. We'll run an open-source runner (we provide the Docker image) that can replay your sample prompts with your desired QPS shape. We will capture server-side metrics (GPU utilization, memory, KV cache hit rate), and client-side latencies.
[06:20] Elena: Important callouts: 1) tokenization differences matter — we will tokenize with the same tokenizer as the model. If your tokenizer differs, we'll align. 2) for long-context requests we measure KV cache warmup; so runs should include a warmup ramp of at least 30 min to populate caches.
[06:44] Mark: For the runner, can we limit egress? Our infra team wants to cap the max simultaneous outbound connections during test.
[06:55] Jordan: Yes, the runner can be configured for concurrency and socket limits. We'll provide sample configs.
[07:10] Priya: On QPS modeling — we've got diurnal patterns, but the critical piece is concurrency and bursts. I want to make sure the POC shows how Redwood handles a sudden 10x spike on short prompts, even if only for 3–7 minutes.
[07:30] Elena: We'll include a synthetic spike profile: baseline at your 99th percentile steady QPS for 40 minutes, then a 6-minute 10x spike, then recovery. We'll run that sequence multiple times in the 48-hour window to see repeatability.
[07:45] Alex: Are you able to simulate token distribution randomness? Some requests attach long documents that cause token variance.
[07:55] Elena: Yes — the runner supports a distribution file where you specify per-request input token count and expected output token count, either as buckets or a sample list. Provide the histogram and we'll replay accordingly.
[08:10] Priya: We'll provide two histograms: one for extraction (short output heavy) and one for summarization (longer output).
[08:18] Samir: Good. Now, model selection: which models are you evaluating? Priya, do you have constraints on model family?
[08:30] Priya: We care about answer quality for entity extraction; currently using an open model (we're evaluating 13B vs 70B variants) and have tuned prompts. We want Redwood to test both an optimized 13B quantized variant and a 70B fp16 or quantized variant if available. Cost delta is important — show cost per 1M tokens for each.
[08:58] Jordan: For 13B we can run quantized int8 profiles which reduce memory and allow higher concurrency. For 70B we'd recommend a multi-GPU configuration; we'll show both in the proposal.
[09:15] Mark: For multi-GPU, do you do tensor-slicing or model parallelism? We need to know network comms overhead.
[09:22] Elena: We use a mix depending on architecture — optimized kernel paths for sharded models and NCCL-based allreduce for larger sequences. We'll surface GPU-to-GPU bandwidth and expected cross-node latency in the run results.
[09:38] Priya: Another gating item — cold start behavior. Some of our flows are infrequent but latency-sensitive. We'll want to see cold-start p95 for a policy that scales up from zero.
[09:52] Elena: We'll include a zero-to-one test: deploy idle pool and then fire a burst to exercise scale-up, measure cold-start time and error rates. Note Dedicated with reserved capacity can avoid cold starts, but we can test autoscaling policies too.
[10:12] Samir: On the instrumentation side we'll deliver trace IDs so you can map requests end-to-end. We'll also include token-level cost logs.
[10:23] Luis: Will you attach GPU utilization per-request? We want to see how requests correlate with GPU load.
[10:28] Elena: Yes, our profiler can annotate GPU metrics with request IDs during the benchmark window. Export format is CSV/Parquet.
[10:40] Priya: For acceptance, we want to ensure model/regression checks are in place — it's possible a quantized 13B changes extraction accuracy. How will we validate quality?
[10:55] Jordan: Two approaches: 1) run an eval set (gold labels) through each model variant and compute extraction F1/precision/recall; 2) inline A/B across a sample of production traffic during the POC if you permit. We'll produce a quality delta report alongside perf numbers.
[11:15] Priya: We'll do the eval set first; we may allow a small shadow A/B later.
[11:23] Alex: Timeline-wise, what's realistic for us to get results?
[11:30] Samir: Tentative timeline: by 2025-08-21 Redwood shares runner and cost template; customer uploads data by 2025-08-22; test window 48 hours starting 2025-08-26; analysis and results 2 business days after; follow-up on 2025-08-29. That fits a 6–7 business day POC loop.
[11:58] Mark: That works if our infra team can provision the peering and firewall exceptions in time. We'll prioritize.
[12:05] Anika: On compliance: we need assurance on log retention and audit logs. Does Redwood provide KMS integration for Dedicated?
[12:15] Jordan: Yes Dedicated supports customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) and we can disable console-level storage for the trial if required. We'll provide SOC2 summary and our security whitepaper.
[12:32] Priya: Great. A couple of detailed asks: 1) show p50/p95/p99 latencies broken down by input token bucket, 2) show tokenized cost per request bucket, 3) show cache hit rates over time, 4) show GPU utilization per-second for the spike windows.
[12:52] Elena: We'll instrument all of that. Also we'll include request-size vs latency scatterplots so you can visualize tail behavior for long-context requests.
[13:05] Samir: For the synthetic spikes, do you want us to also vary output token sizes to test worst-case compute per token?
[13:12] Priya: Yes, please — the worst-case for us is long-input + long-output, which is compute-heavy. Include at least two worst-case windows.
[13:24] Elena: Noted. Now a practical question: dataset privacy during the trial. You said you'll anonymize PII; will that affect token distribution?
[13:35] Priya: It might but we can token-stub (replace names with single tokens) which preserves token counts closely. We'll add a note explaining our sanitizer approach.
[13:45] Samir: Helpful. Regarding success criteria again, can we write that down? Priya — you said p50 < 200–300ms for short prompts and p95 < 1s. Anything else?
[13:58] Priya: Also cost target within 30% of current spend, error rate <5% during spikes, and model F1 drop < 2% when moving to quantized 13B vs baseline.
[14:15] Jordan: We'll produce a one-page acceptance matrix mapping those to measured metrics.
[14:22] Mark: On cost reporting — will you show amortized cost per 1M tokens and per 10k requests?
[14:30] Elena: Yes, both. We'll attach a CSV that breaks down cost per model variant and per bucket.
[14:38] Alex: Is there any recommended client-side rate limiting to avoid thundering herd?
[14:44] Jordan: For burst mitigation we recommend a token-based shedder or adaptive client backoff. For the POC we'll simulate both unthrottled and client-throttled spike runs so you can compare.
[15:00] Priya: Regarding metrics retention — how long will these logs be available? For analysis we want 30 days.
[15:10] Elena: For the trial we can retain logs for 30 days in your S3; console retention is 7 days, but we can extend on request for the trial window.
[15:20] Anika: Please also include an export of audit logs for the trial. We'll run them through our compliance checks.
[15:30] Samir: We'll include an audit log bundle with every benchmark export.
[15:38] Luis: One more ops question: if the 48-hour run causes GPU contention and we see OOMs, what's the remediation path?
[15:48] Jordan: We'll have fallback policies: scale-up to reserved burst capacity (if applicable), fallback to a smaller model variant, or shed large requests to a queue. We'll test automatic fallback during one of the run attempts. We'll record the exact behavior.
[16:05] Priya: OK that's important. Also will you instrument queue lengths and per-request retry counts?
[16:12] Elena: Yes queue lengths, retry counts, and backpressure indicators will be in the perf logs.
[16:20] Alex: For the POC results deck — we want a recommended production footprint and cost forecast for steady state and for 99th percentile day; can you include headroom recommendations?
[16:32] Samir: Yes, that's part of the deliverable. We'll provide recommended pool sizes and autoscale targets to meet the SLOs.
[16:40] Priya: Any constraints on how you will run the quantized 13B vs 70B? For fairness, same seed and prompt templates?
[16:48] Elena: We'll fix seeds for deterministic sampling where applicable, and run the exact same prompt set. For sampling differences we'll report perplexity and token-level differences.
[17:00] Mark: Do you support streaming responses for our summarization flows?
[17:06] Jordan: Yes, streaming is available and we'll measure stream latency as well as final completion latency.
[17:12] Priya: For the spike windows, we want to see how streaming degrades — sometimes streaming helps perceived latency.
[17:20] Elena: We'll include both streaming and non-streaming comparisons.
[17:30] Samir: Quick note on cost centers — we'll provide per-route cost; if you have different product routes we can map them to separate tags.
[17:38] Alex: Yes map them to our internal routes — extraction-prod, summary-prod.
[17:45] Priya: One more thing: consider warm vs cold KV cache scenarios per customer tenant day. Our tenants have different prompt reuse; how granular can you make caching metrics?
[17:56] Elena: We can tag cache metrics by tenant id if you provide a tenant field during the test data. We'll anonymize tenant IDs but preserve distribution.
[18:10] Priya: We'll add that to the dataset.
[18:18] Samir: Alright, to recap real quick — deliverables from Redwood: benchmark runner + Docker image, cost modeling spreadsheet, sample config for spike/steady profiles, instrumentation list, security whitepaper and SOC2 excerpt. From Sentinel: sample prompts + token histograms, networking details, and go-ahead for the 48-hour window.
[18:40] Priya: Correct. We'll aim to get the data in the bucket Friday.
[18:45] Mark: We'll prioritize firewall/peering.
[18:48] Anika: I'll review the security materials once you send them.
[18:52] Samir: Great. Any final questions?
[19:00] Luis: One small nit: for the 48-hour run do you need dedicated GPUs reserved or will Redwood allocate burst capacity?
[19:10] Jordan: We'll use reserved Dedicated pools for predictable throughput; if you choose Dedicated trial you'll get a predictable baseline. We'll propose a small reserved pool for the run and have optional burst to handle extra load.
[19:25] Priya: We'll budget for that.
[19:30] Samir: Okay, we'll send the proposal and runner tomorrow. Thanks everyone, will follow up with links.
[19:36] Priya: Thanks, appreciate it.
[19:38] Alex: Thanks all.
[19:40] Samir: End call.

Post-call notes (auto):
- Customer to provide token histogram and sample prompts.
- Redwood to prepare 48-hour test plan and provide runner and cost template.
- Security and network gating to be completed prior to test window.

Transcript notes: transcription contains occasional recognition errors (names, acronyms). Natural speech artifacts present.

Bench plan (short outline included in transcript body):
1) Warmup: 30-minute ramp at baseline QPS to warm caches.
2) Steady-state windows: 6 windows of 2 hours at 90th-percentile QPS.
3) Spike tests: 4x sequences where we do a 6-minute 10x spike and 20-minute recovery. Two of those sequences will include worst-case long-context requests.
4) Cold-start test: idle pool then single burst to measure cold-start p95.
5) Model variants: quantized 13B, 13B fp16 baseline (if available), 70B sharded variant.
6) Metrics: per-request latency (p50/p95/p99), GPU util, cache hit rate, token cost per bucket, error rate, audit logs export.

Acceptance matrix (summary):
- Latency: short prompts p50 < 300ms, p95 < 1s
- Reliability: error rate < 5% during spikes
- Cost: within 30% of current per-token spend for acceptable quality model
- Quality: quantized 13B F1 drop < 2% vs baseline

References & links mentioned:
- Redwood benchmark runner (link to be shared)
- Security whitepaper and SOC2 excerpt (link to be shared)
- Shared S3 bucket path (to be confirmed)
notes: Customer asked for per-token cost CSV and headroom recommendations
Redwood to include streaming vs non-streaming comparisons
Customer will provide anonymized tokenized prompts
